article.title: Goodhart’s Law: When a Useful Metric Becomes a Bad Target
article.why: Deep Dive on KPI design, incentives, and unintended behavior.

paragraphs.en:
Metrics help organizations turn broad goals into something observable. A customer service team may track response time, a sales team may track revenue, and a product team may track daily active users. The problem begins when a useful measure becomes a target that people are strongly rewarded for hitting. Goodhart's Law is commonly summarized as the idea that when a measure becomes a target, it can stop being a good measure.

Consider a call center that wants to improve customer experience. Managers notice that long waiting times are associated with complaints, so they set a target for shorter calls. Agents quickly learn to end conversations faster. Average handling time falls, and the dashboard looks better. But some customers need to call again because their problems were not fully solved. The metric improved while the underlying objective—effective service—may have worsened.

This does not mean targets are useless. It means incentives change behavior. Once employees know exactly how performance is measured, they naturally adapt their actions to the measurement system. Sometimes this adaptation is desirable. Other times it creates gaming, shortcuts, or substitution: people optimize the measured dimension while sacrificing an unmeasured one.

Sales quotas offer another example. If representatives are rewarded only for the number of new contracts, they may prioritize easy-to-close customers, offer excessive discounts, or sign customers who are likely to cancel. A machine-learning team rewarded only for model accuracy might avoid difficult cases or choose a test set that makes performance look stronger. A growth team judged only by registrations may create promotions that attract low-quality accounts rather than long-term users.

The deeper issue is that most business goals are multidimensional. 'Good customer service' includes speed, resolution quality, fairness, and satisfaction. 'Healthy growth' includes acquisition, retention, margin, and customer value. A single KPI is a proxy for this larger objective. The stronger the incentive attached to the proxy, the greater the temptation to optimize the proxy rather than the real goal.

Better measurement systems therefore combine several practices. First, pair a primary KPI with guardrail metrics. If response time is the target, monitor repeat contacts and satisfaction as guardrails. Second, examine the distribution, not only the average, because teams can sometimes improve an average by neglecting difficult cases. Third, audit qualitative examples. Listening to actual calls or reviewing rejected cases can reveal behavior hidden by aggregate metrics. Fourth, periodically revisit whether the metric still predicts the outcome it was designed to represent.

Goodhart's Law is especially relevant in data-driven organizations because dashboards can create an illusion of objectivity. A precisely measured number is still only a representation of a goal. The right question is not simply, 'Did the KPI improve?' It is, 'What behavior did this KPI encourage, what important dimensions are missing, and did the real-world outcome improve as well?'

Targets can also create threshold effects. If a branch receives a bonus for keeping complaints below 2 percent, managers may treat a movement from 2.1 to 1.9 percent as far more important than an equally large improvement elsewhere. They may also debate which cases count as complaints. This is a warning sign that the operational definition has become economically valuable in itself. Strong governance therefore documents definitions, prevents convenient reclassification, and reviews sudden KPI improvements for changes in process or measurement. When a metric jumps immediately after an incentive changes, the organization should ask whether performance improved, reporting behavior changed, or both. The goal is not to distrust employees; it is to design a system in which doing the right thing for customers also tends to improve the measured outcome.

translations.zh: 重點翻譯：Goodhart’s Law 提醒我們，當一個原本有用的 measure 被直接設成強力考核 target，人們會開始最佳化這個 proxy，而不一定最佳化真正的 business objective。解法不是不用 KPI，而是搭配 guardrail metrics、看 distribution、抽查 qualitative cases，並定期驗證 KPI 是否仍能代表真正成果。
translations.ja: 要点訳：有用な指標でも、強い評価目標にすると、人は本来の目的ではなくproxyそのものを最適化し始めることがある。KPIを捨てるのではなく、guardrail metric、分布、定性レビューを組み合わせ、指標と実際の成果の関係を定期的に見直す必要がある。

vocabulary.usage: A strong incentive can change how people respond to a metric.
The underlying objective may worsen even when the metric improves.

vocabulary.ja: 指標の抜け道を利用する行動
vocabulary.usage: Gaming occurs when people exploit measurement rules without improving the goal.
Metric substitution replaces the real goal with an easier measured proxy.
A sales quota can encourage unintended contract behavior.
Customer service is a multidimensional objective.
A KPI is often a proxy for a broader business goal.
Guardrail metrics detect harm created while optimizing the primary KPI.
Aggregate metrics can hide poor outcomes for difficult cases.
Qualitative review can reveal behavior that a dashboard misses.
Precise dashboards can create an illusion of objectivity.

business.term: Pair the primary KPI with guardrails that capture unintended harm.
business.explanation: 主要 KPI 要搭配能捕捉副作用的 guardrail。

business.term: Revalidate whether the proxy still represents the business outcome.
business.explanation: 定期重新確認 proxy 是否仍代表真正 business outcome。
